How Do You Design Triangulation Within a Case Study?

Should the interviews, documents, and observations confirm the same findings? What if administrators describe extensive faculty consultation while faculty members report that major decisions had already been made? Does disagreement indicate a methodological weakness, or could it reveal something important about the case?

Triangulation is frequently invoked as evidence of qualitative rigor, yet its analytical procedures are often left unspecified. A defensible case study needs to explain not only which evidence sources will be collected, but also how they will be compared, interpreted, and used to evaluate the study's claims.

To design triangulation within a case study, identify the claims or phenomena that require examination, select evidence sources or analytical perspectives capable of informing them, and specify how agreements, differences, and contradictions will be evaluated.

Triangulation may involve different data sources, methods, investigators, or theoretical perspectives. Its purpose is not necessarily to make all evidence agree. Depending on the research tradition, triangulation may strengthen corroboration, reveal contrasting meanings, expose limitations in particular sources, or produce a more nuanced interpretation of the bounded case.
What Does Triangulation Mean in Case Study Research?

In case study research, triangulation is particularly relevant because the case often involves multiple actors, processes, and contextual conditions that cannot be adequately understood from one perspective alone.
For example, an institutional policy may exist as a formal document, be interpreted differently by faculty members, and be implemented inconsistently across departments.
Each perspective provides information about a different aspect of the case.

Denzin's influential typology distinguishes data, investigator, theory, and methodological triangulation. Yin emphasizes converging lines of evidence as an important feature of case study inquiry, while Stake's interpretive approach gives considerable attention to understanding the case through multiple perspectives.

For example, a claim that faculty consultation influenced policy revisions could be examined through participant accounts, consultation records, successive policy drafts, and documented decision sequences.

Use triangulation whenever a conclusion matters enough that someone will question it, and whenever a single method could plausibly have produced the result on its own. Triangulation requires more than collecting interviews, documents, and observations. Learn how to design meaningful comparisons across evidence, investigate disagreements, avoid false corroboration, and establish what different sources can legitimately support.
In the methodology, you write that triangulation will be achieved through multiple data sources. But what happens after those sources have been collected?

Triangulation is frequently invoked as evidence of qualitative rigor, yet its analytical procedures are often left unspecified. A defensible case study needs to explain not only which evidence sources will be collected, but also how they will be compared, interpreted, and used to evaluate the study's claims.
Design Triangulation Around Claims, Evidence Relationships, and Competing Interpretations

To design triangulation within a case study, identify the claims or phenomena that require examination, select evidence sources or analytical perspectives capable of informing them, and specify how agreements, differences, and contradictions will be evaluated.

Triangulation may involve different data sources, methods, investigators, or theoretical perspectives. Its purpose is not necessarily to make all evidence agree. Depending on the research tradition, triangulation may strengthen corroboration, reveal contrasting meanings, expose limitations in particular sources, or produce a more nuanced interpretation of the bounded case.

Use triangulation whenever a conclusion matters enough that someone will question it, and whenever a single method could plausibly have produced the result on its own. To design triangulation within a case study, identify the claims or phenomena that require examination, select evidence sources or analytical perspectives capable of informing them, and specify how agreements, differences, and contradictions will be evaluated.

Triangulation refers to examining a phenomenon through different sources of evidence, methods, investigators, or theoretical perspectives to develop a more informed understanding.
